title: The Logic of Small Bets for Big Wins Is Dead. We're Now Building Jurassic Rodents
dek: On the fundraising side and the exit side, dollar VC has been cut off at both ends; the leverage story of two or three hits out of ten checks no longer holds. CMC Capital's (清流资本) answer: either invest in the present — one to two years to cash out — or in the future, seven to ten years out. The middle ground is the hardest.
why: A partner at a small dual-currency (RMB + USD) fund describes, very concretely, what the last two years have actually been like in VC: fundraising, exits, chaotic round structures, valuation logic, shifting founder standards. Information density is medium-high; the second half, on robotics and the aging economy, is worth more.
who: Investors tracking the real survival conditions of China's primary market, hard-tech and AI founders thinking about the pacing of their next raise, and practitioners who want to understand how the rules of the VC game are changing.
skip: After 1:13:50, the chat about the human comedy of a downturn — low information density.

points.h: Dividend strategies are really debt in equity's clothing, and they're hard to do
points.body: One camp, represented by Zhu Xiaohu, has figured it out: the old VC logic of small bets for big wins simply doesn't hold, so they've turned to cash flow — investing in companies with revenue, profit, and the ability to pay dividends, where the exit doesn't even have to be an IPO. But Mengqiu points out this becomes debt in equity's clothing, and those deals aren't easy either — you have to run into a company that already has good revenue and cash flow and still wants to raise. Why would a company that can actually make money dilute its equity to raise? So you can only count on luck. She sees it as a clear enough strategy, not right or wrong, but fundamentally a phase — because the VC financial product was never meant to do this from day one.

points.h: Robot bodies are too expensive, so everyone can only spread their bets
points.body: Mengqiu's personal judgment is that robotics is the direction where AI meets the physical world. Whether or not this generation of technology can truly understand the physical world, this generation of AI's real value has to show up in combination with the physical world to unlock productivity. But robot body companies are extremely expensive from the start — a single deal takes too much money, and no one can fund it alone, so each investor's money only stretches to two or three companies, and in the end maybe two or three survive, or even just one — a one-in-two or one-in-three shot. She endorses Wang Haodong's strategy of investing in all three, because Jinqiao Robotics (金桥机器人) invested in Li Auto, holds a clear deployment scenario in hand, and the logic of looking up and down the new-energy-vehicle chain — materials, batteries, components — can be replicated in robotics.

points.h: The earlier a shareholder is, the harder it is to exit, and they have little bargaining power
points.body: From her own experience exiting projects, Mengqiu draws a counterintuitive conclusion: the earlier you get in, the harder it is to get out. Because if you want to negotiate terms like repurchase, you have to negotiate them in every subsequent round, and since later investors put in more money, early shareholders actually have no bargaining power. So when CMC Capital (清流资本) first started looking at this generation of AI technology a year and a half ago, it drafted its own research framework and quickly concluded: don't look at large models, and don't favor anyone other than the big platforms building large models. Her plain theory: if OpenAI hadn't had Microsoft, it might have died on the road long ago; even now OpenAI's own ability to generate revenue is far behind its ability to spend, and that's with Microsoft already handing it a massive deployment scenario.

points.h: The fool's window the big platforms used to leave open is gone
points.body: Mengqiu argues that many startup teams' opportunities came from a fool's window — the big platforms weren't awake yet. But with this generation of generative AI, the big platforms were awake from day one. They have plenty of money, they're not behind on thinking, and they have their own application scenarios and data feedback loops. So third-party startup teams building foundation models don't have much of a chance. She originally thought multimodal large models had a time window — the big platforms were too busy to do it, and startups could at least sell to everyone. But after Sora came out this spring, she felt the concept of an independent multimodal large model no longer holds, because all foundation models are fusing more modalities, and an independent multimodal model essentially still needs to call on a language model's comprehension ability.

points.h: Only pushing something to the extreme can succeed; the middle ground is the hardest
points.body: Mengqiu sums up her own investment philosophy: push something to the extreme — clear enough, crazy enough, walking unswervingly in one direction — and it can succeed; the middle ground is very hard, and there may be no success in the middle ground at all. This explains why she bets on both ends — either invest in the present, with immediate results, making money next year or the year after, or invest in the future, seven to ten years out, and not in the transitional middle. She applies the same framework to the AI application layer: voice is an underestimated link, because everyone naturally assumes the voice market is small, pays it little attention, and is still messing around with text, images, and video — but when AIGC reaches real scenarios in the future, voice will matter, and it needs to reach the point where, like in the film Her, you immediately feel a real person is speaking.

points.h: You now make money on consensus, not on non-consensus
points.body: Mengqiu points to a key shift: VC used to make money on non-consensus; now it has to make money on consensus. Because there's limited money in the market, everyone has to believe in one direction for everyone to be willing to keep putting money in. When there's a lot of money, chaos is allowed; when there's little, it isn't. So she redefines VC as No Venture — we are not Venture, we want not to take risks, to avoid risk as much as possible. On the future end, you invest in what everyone believes, in consensus, which is relatively lower risk; on the other end, it's what can be cashed out immediately. Two extremes, no middle ground.

points.h: Be a Jurassic-era rodent: survive first
points.body: Mengqiu uses a metaphor: when the asteroid hit, the dinosaurs all died, but mammals, which had been very small next to reptiles, a disadvantaged group, survived the catastrophe. She says she isn't saying today's giants will die, but overall the giants take a bigger hit. So CMC Capital wants to be a Jurassic-era rodent — a mouse, living in the gutter, with a smaller range and less food, but not lying flat. She turned down an offer from a local government guidance fund, because those funds come with a great many requirements — how to define the reinvestment ratio, the investment direction has to be set in advance — and she feels that in the current situation it's better to keep control over the money in her own hands.

points.h: The new-era VC logic: PE equals 10, and rounds no longer matter
points.body: Mengqiu says primary-market valuations are now very clear: PE equals 10, because the secondary market is only giving 15; when the secondary market gives 30, PE equals 15. Rounds have also become chaotic, because the VC logic no longer holds — it's no longer a round-by-round game of passing the parcel to push valuations up. Projects that can actually make money within a year or two don't lack money themselves; they may have raised only one round in their history, or never raised at all, and just want to bring in some funds for endorsement. Such projects are very sparse, but CMC Capital invests in few projects anyway — it may look at a hundred and find one. The criteria for the present are more diversified; the criteria for the future are still long-term value, seven to ten years.
